### Background
* Before this change, even on non-AWS platforms, the Enabled() check attempts
  to make calls to the metadata endpoint when the session and credentials
  are initialized (in order to determine if the provider should be
  initialized at all).
* This can cause latency because the SDK times out and retries -- up to
  20 seconds of latency has been observed on non-AWS platforms when the
  metadata IP was blocked with an iptables rule.
* Instead, check once if we are running on an EC2 platform, first trying
  to find the EC2 UUID in system files, and second attempting to get
  credentials.
* Add a benchmark test that includes intialization and the credential
  check.

### Benchmark Results

        For verbose messaging see aws.Config.CredentialsChainVerboseErrors
[...]

beep boop @nckturner @andrewsykim :upside_down_face:

On second thought, this could be misleading because kubelet will always attempt to authenticate to ECR repos but `Provide` will fail if there's no session established. Could `Enabled` instead check the availablility of the metadata server and/or the aws credentials on disk `~/.aws/credentials`? Basically a similar check to what already exists but skips the API calls.
FYI @liggitt

/priority important-soon
/sig cloud-provider
sorry this escaped attention for so long. agree this should be fixed asap.
Will address the comments

> we'd need to check everything in the sdk's credential chain

Is there a way to configure the client to check everything in the SDK credential chain except for those that require API calls? And if so, is that a sufficient enough check?

@andrewsykim It could be retries to IMDS that is causing the latency when we try to set up the session. There is logic in the SDK which has to decide between IMDSv1 and IMDSv2, with a fallback mechanism.  There have been issues in the past with the SDK which caused latency when falling back to IMDSv1.  If this is the case, then we might be able to get rid of the latency just adjusting the timeout.  

The other possibility is, the SDK sees the service account token and then tries to do an assume-role-with-web-identity call, which it can use to exchange for aws creds.  I'll see if I can pinpoint the latency. (Edit: actually I don't think this would happen if the env var `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` isn't set.)

@andrewsykim I repro'd this on a gce instance (although that might have not been necessary, given the repro).  If you drop packets to the metadata endpoint via an iptables rule, the aws sdk gets really unhappy:  

```
root@kubernetes-build:/home/nic/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws# sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -o ens4 -d 169.254.169.254/32 -j DROP
root@kubernetes-build:/home/nic/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws# telnet 169.254.169.254 80
Trying 169.254.169.254...
^C
root@kubernetes-build:/home/nic/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws# go test -bench .
E1120 07:51:03.065014    9083 aws_credentials.go:69] aws_credential:1
E1120 07:51:03.065656    9083 aws_credentials.go:73] aws_credential:2
E1120 07:51:03.065686    9083 aws_credentials.go:78] aws_credential:3
E1120 07:51:23.405789    9083 aws_credentials.go:80] aws_credential:4
E1120 07:51:23.405826    9083 aws_credentials.go:81] while getting AWS credentials NoCredentialProviders: no valid providers in chain. Deprecated.
        For verbose messaging see aws.Config.CredentialsChainVerboseErrors
ECR is enabled: false
goos: linux
goarch: amd64
pkg: k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws
BenchmarkSetupLatency-8                1        20340895511 ns/op
PASS
ok      k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws    20.358s
root@kubernetes-build:/home/nic/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws# 

```

This is the patch I used to test: 
```
nic@kubernetes-build:~/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws$ git diff
diff --git a/pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials.go b/pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials.go
index a650a7da50b..3a06d9ea7b3 100644
--- a/pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials.go
+++ b/pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials.go
@@ -66,17 +66,22 @@ func newECRProvider(getterFactory tokenGetterFactory) *ecrProvider {
 // Enabled implements DockerConfigProvider.Enabled. Enabled is true if AWS
 // credentials are found.
 func (p *ecrProvider) Enabled() bool {
+       klog.Error("aws_credential:1")
        sess, err := session.NewSessionWithOptions(session.Options{
                SharedConfigState: session.SharedConfigEnable,
        })
+       klog.Error("aws_credential:2")
        if err != nil {
                klog.Errorf("while validating AWS credentials %v", err)
                return false
        }
+       klog.Error("aws_credential:3")
        if _, err := sess.Config.Credentials.Get(); err != nil {
+               klog.Error("aws_credential:4")
                klog.Errorf("while getting AWS credentials %v", err)
                return false
        }
+       klog.Error("aws_credential:5")
        return true
 }
 
diff --git a/pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials_test.go b/pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials_test.go
index 7161fc136d1..27536acce20 100644
--- a/pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials_test.go
+++ b/pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials_test.go
@@ -331,3 +331,9 @@ func TestChinaECRProvideCached(t *testing.T) {
                t.Errorf("cached credentials do not match")
        }
 }
+
+func BenchmarkSetupLatency(b *testing.B) {
+       p := newECRProvider(&ecrTokenGetterFactory{cache: make(map[string]tokenGetter)})
+       enabled := p.Enabled()
+       fmt.Printf("ECR is enabled: %v\n", enabled)
+}

```

Without the iptables rule, the benchmark takes about 30 milliseconds:
```
ok      k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws    0.031s
```
and from a network namespace without any connectivity: 
```
root@kubernetes-build:/home/nic/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws# ip netns exec test0 go test -bench .
...
ok      k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/credentialprovider/aws    0.021s

```
Its about 10 ms faster then the default case, probably because it immediately fails because there is no interface. (20 ms is still a long time though...)

Anyway, this is all to say, I don't think we can rely on the SDK or configure it to only check "the fast things" since instance metadata is pretty central to what it tries to do.  Using `-j REJECT` instead of `-j DROP brings the latency down to 4-6 seconds (depending on version of sdk), but that's still unacceptable. I think I'm leaning toward's @liggitt's solution of a run once check, the only thing I don't like about it is that if the metadata check randomly fails for an AWS kubelet, then that kubelet would have to be restarted (if I'm understanding correctly).

> the only thing I don't like about it is that if the metadata check randomly fails for an AWS kubelet, then that kubelet would have to be restarted (if I'm understanding correctly).

Yeah this would be problematic -- a failed connection to metadata server would disable the provider indefinitely, but we can't necessary panic either,  otherwise kubelets that are not on EC2 instances would panic too.

> the only thing I don't like about it is that if the metadata check randomly fails for an AWS kubelet, then that kubelet would have to be restarted (if I'm understanding correctly).

it would be nice if that could be improved, but I see that as something for the AWS provider to work on as a follow-up after getting this merged to avoid affecting all non-AWS deployments
Having a hard time understanding how the run once check helps here. `Enabled()` is a blocking call and even if we ran it once it would block kubelet startup anyways?

> move the current Enabled() check to a once.Do check we call before calling getFromECR. If that fails, make future calls to Provide() no-op

Ah, because we would move the check to `Provide()` and we have `Enabled` always return true.

Well this makes me think we should just have `Enabled()` return true and rely on the regex to short circuit any non-ecr images, like it was before.  Then, only if the user is actually trying to pull an ECR image, do we actually attempt to set up aws credentials.  This means that the only users who would experience the latency are those who: 1. are trying to pull an ECR image and 2. don't have any valid (accessible via the credential chain) aws credentials set up and 3. have blocked access to metadata.  That way, aws users can experience a metadata outage and not have to deal with restarting kubelets across their fleets.  Additionally, this shouldn't be a problem once we get to external credential providers, since the ecr provider doesn't even need to be present on non-aws clusters.

Enabled() is called from NewDockerKeyring()

When used with CRI, this is only called once at startup time from NewKubeGenericRuntimeManager(), so AWS nodes with metadata unavailable at kubelet start already had their AWS credential provider disabled.

When used with dockershim, this is called on every image pull from ensureSandboxImageExists()

While limiting the impact to Provide() and scoping to ECR images is clearly better than the current code for dockershim, I don't think we should re-add a check on every pull to kubelets using CRI on non-AWS nodes.

I guess what you're saying is its gross to make "Enabled" meaningless in the CRI code path, and cause every image pull to check with the ecr credential provider, even if its protected by the image uri regex, because it exposes clusters running on other providers to bugs in the ecr credential provider, and could be considered an anti-pattern to execute this provider specific code path when its unnecessary.  

But I would argue if you look at the negatives for each approach, comparing how each affects aws users and non-aws users, the downside to all aws users in the event of a metadata outage at the wrong time is much worse in the short-circuit approach (requires intervention by cluster operators) than the downside of non-aws users being exposed to future code bugs and having code path execute that is unnecessary in the run-once approach (unless I'm missing other downsides).  Additionally, this is remediated by the new credential provider framework, so this isn't something permanent, either.  Given that, I'd ask if we can go back to using the regex short-circuit on every CRI image pull.

If we still want to go with a run-once check, maybe we can first check for the "EC2" prefix in each of:
```
sh-4.2$ cat /sys/hypervisor/uuid 
ec2106d7-184d-6e02-7a1b-00fcc21b0741

sh-4.2$ sudo cat /sys/devices/virtual/dmi/id/product_uuid 
EC2106D7-184D-6E02-7A1B-00FCC21B0741
```
and only attempt metadata/credential chain if those fail or or don't exist, which would make most ec2 checks work even during a metadata outage or flake.

Those files look promising. Avoiding perma-failure due to unavailable metadata where one of those files positively indicates we are in ec2 seems reasonable, as long as we get the following characteristics on non-EC2 nodes (nodes where those files are missing and/or do not contain ec2/EC2):

* Enabled() is fast and doesn't make API calls
* Provide(non-ECR image) is fast and doesn't make API calls
* Provide(ECR image) makes a slow failing invocation at most once, then is fast on future invocations and doesn't make API calls

@liggitt I took an initial pass at your comments.

> sure... by moving the existing check to a single run-once that happens only after we are asked to provide credentials for an ECR image, I think we do the following:
> * maintain current behavior on AWS
> * remove lag on non-AWS on a cluster that never tries to pull an ECR image
> * limits lag on a non-AWS cluster that tries to pull an ECR image to a single attempt

As an initial version I did the once.Do in the enabled(), because I think its easier to understand, and the slow call will only happen once on non-AWS kubelets. 

> When used with CRI, this is only called once at startup time

Since it will only be called once at startup time with CRI, I think it would be reasonable, but if you'd prefer I can move it to `Provide()` to account for dockershim.

> the slow call will only happen once on non-AWS kubelets.

there needs to be zero network calls made on a non-AWS kubelet that is not asked to pull an ECR image.
/retest
/retest

/retest
/lgtm
Ready for review @liggitt

/lgtm

issue_context.title: aws credentials provider causes ~10s-20s hangup on kubelet's initializing docker runtime
issue_context.body:
Following commit in 1.15 on aws credentials provider  causes ~10s-20s delay(kubelet main goroutine hangup) on kubelet's initializing docker runtime for nodes of K8s clusters not running on AWS:


[Refactors and fixes bugs in AWS credentialprovider - 11efc013288a](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/11efc013288a15322a6abc0852a4859f7b0785dc)

We observed **20s delay** on our 1.16 production nodes, while on local clusters, the delay is about **9s to 14s**

This commit failed to check whether the node is running on AWS or not before calling AWS APIs. 

Please add this check like other providers, such as GCP,Azure. Thanks.

GCP: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/credentialprovider/gcp/metadata.go#L146
Azure: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/credentialprovider/azure/azure_credentials.go#L157


# Test results
## add trace to pkg/credentialprovider/aws/aws_credentials.go
```
func (p *ecrProvider) Enabled() bool {
	klog.Info("aws_credential:1")
	sess, err := session.NewSessionWithOptions(session.Options{
		SharedConfigState: session.SharedConfigEnable,
	})
	klog.Info("aws_credential:2")
	if err != nil {
		klog.Errorf("while validating AWS credentials %v", err)
		return false
	}
	klog.Info("aws_credential:3")
	if _, err := sess.Config.Credentials.Get(); err != nil {
		klog.Info("aws_credential:4")
		klog.Errorf("while getting AWS credentials %v", err)
		return false
	}
	klog.Info("aws_credential:5")
	return true
}
```

Interesting.  It doesn't have to be perfect, we still try to initialize credentials after doing these checks. The advantage to being able to shortcut the credential checks is that in the case the metadata endpoint is down temporarily, we can still verify the machine is on EC2.  Since we're now using a `once.Do()` check, if the endpoint was down we would disable the provider and the operator would have to restart kubelet.  With these checks, the operator would only have to restart kubelet if these file checks don't work (e.g. little endian), and the credentials fail to initialize because of an outage.

this means that Provide() will be called for all images on all platforms, log v(3) output about the image not being a valid ECR repository URL for non-ECR images, and try to acquire ECR credentials for images matching the ECR regex.

sure... by moving the existing check to a single run-once that happens only after we are asked to provide credentials for an ECR image, I *think* we do the following:
* maintain current behavior on AWS
* remove lag on non-AWS on a cluster that never tries to pull an ECR image
* limits lag on a non-AWS cluster that tries to pull an ECR image to a single attempt
